Hair Services

Hair Extensions: What to Know

Home / Hair Services / Hair Extensions

Extensions add length, volume, or both, but the method matters as much as the hair itself. Different application techniques suit different hair types, budgets, and lifestyles, and choosing the wrong one for your situation is the most common reason people end up unhappy with the result. This guide covers the main methods, what upkeep actually looks like, and the questions worth asking before you commit.

Common Methods

  • Tape-in: thin wefts adhered with medical-grade tape, typically reset every 6–8 weeks. Popular for being relatively fast to apply and gentle on fine hair.
  • Sew-in / weft: wefts sewn onto braided tracks, common for adding significant length or volume. Requires enough natural hair density to braid a secure base.
  • Clip-in: temporary, removable extensions you apply and remove yourself, ideal for occasional wear without a salon appointment.
  • Fusion / keratin bond: individual strands bonded with heat, longer-lasting but more involved to apply and remove — often the most natural-looking option but also the most time-intensive.
  • Micro-link / beaded: strands attached with small metal beads rather than heat or tape, which some people prefer to avoid heat-based bonding altogether.

Matching Method to Hair Type

Fine or thin hair generally does best with lighter-weight methods like tape-ins, since heavier techniques can put more tension on individual strands and increase breakage risk. Thicker, more resilient hair has more flexibility to carry sew-in wefts or fusion bonds without as much strain. If you have a history of hair breakage or a sensitive scalp, mention that during your consultation — an experienced stylist will often steer you toward a gentler method even if it's not the one you originally asked about.

Upkeep

Most methods require periodic salon visits to move or replace the extensions as your natural hair grows, along with gentle brushing — starting from the ends and working up — and sulfate-free products at home. Sleeping with hair loosely braided can help reduce tangling and matting around the attachment points overnight, which is one of the most common sources of frustration with extensions in the first few weeks.

What Extensions Cost Over Time

It's worth thinking about extensions as an ongoing cost, not a one-time purchase. Beyond the initial application, most methods require maintenance appointments every 6–10 weeks, and the hair itself may eventually need to be replaced or supplemented depending on the quality and how well it's cared for. Ask your stylist for a realistic estimate of the total cost over six months to a year, not just the price of the first appointment.

Questions to Ask Before Booking

  • Which method do you recommend for my hair density, texture, and goals?
  • What's the expected maintenance schedule and cost over time?
  • What hair quality and source do you use, and can I see samples?
  • How should I sleep, wash, and style my hair differently once extensions are in?

Signs It's Time to Remove Extensions

Extensions shouldn't be left in indefinitely regardless of method — most manufacturers and stylists recommend a maximum wear time before removal and reapplication, both to protect your natural hair and because the attachment points naturally loosen as hair grows. Matting near the roots, visible slippage, or noticeable tension or discomfort are all signs it's time for a removal and reassessment rather than pushing past the recommended timeline.

Removal Should Also Be Professional

It's worth booking removal with a professional rather than attempting it yourself, especially for bonded or taped methods — the solvents and techniques used to safely release adhesive or bonds are specifically designed to avoid pulling on natural hair, and DIY removal is one of the more common ways people end up with unexpected breakage or damage from an otherwise well-maintained set of extensions.
